questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given phrase.

A person who scientifically studies the stars, planets, and other celestial bodies.

options.option_text: Astrologer
Astronomer
Astronaut
Agronomist

questions.explanation: An 'Astronomer' is a scientist who studies astronomy, dealing with celestial objects and space. An 'Astrologer' predicts the future based on star positions, an 'Astronaut' travels to space, and an 'Agronomist' studies soil management and crop production.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given phrase.

A dedicated place where books, documents, and records are systematically kept for reading and reference.

options.option_text: Museum
Archive
Library
Granary

questions.explanation: A 'Library' is the standard collection of books for reading and reference. An 'Archive' is specifically for historical documents or public records. A 'Museum' stores historical artifacts, and a 'Granary' is a storehouse for threshed grain.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given phrase.

A person who strongly and annoyingly insists on strict adherence to formal rules or literal meaning, especially in academic learning.

options.option_text: Scholar
Novice
Zealot
Pedant

questions.explanation: A 'Pedant' is someone who is excessively concerned with minor details and rules or with displaying academic learning. A 'Scholar' is simply a learned person, a 'Novice' is a beginner, and a 'Zealot' is a fanatic.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given phrase.

A piece of handwriting that is so messy or unclear that it cannot be easily read.

options.option_text: Illegible
Infallible
Invincible
Inaudible

questions.explanation: 'Illegible' refers specifically to text or handwriting that is impossible or very hard to read. 'Infallible' means incapable of making mistakes, 'Invincible' means too powerful to be defeated, and 'Inaudible' means unable to be heard.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given phrase.

A hypothetical remedy or cure that is supposed to heal all diseases and solve all problems.

options.option_text: Placebo
Antidote
Panacea
Narcotic

questions.explanation: A 'Panacea' (from Greek pan 'all' + akos 'remedy') is a solution or remedy for all difficulties or diseases. A 'Placebo' is a harmless pill prescribed for psychological benefit. An 'Antidote' neutralizes specific poisons.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given phrase.

The horrific act of intentionally killing one's own brother or sister.

options.option_text: Patricide
Fratricide
Sororicide
Regicide

questions.explanation: 'Fratricide' comes from Latin 'frater' (brother) and 'cida' (killer), meaning the killing of one's brother (and sometimes extended to sister). 'Patricide' is killing a father, 'Sororicide' strictly a sister, and 'Regicide' killing a king.

questions.stem:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given phrase.

A person who is highly disciplined and totally indifferent to both physical pleasure and pain.

options.option_text: Cynic
Ascetic
Mystic
Stoic

questions.explanation: A 'Stoic' is a person who endures hardship and pain without complaining or showing emotion, rooted in ancient Greek Stoicism. An 'Ascetic' practices severe self-discipline for religious reasons. A 'Cynic' believes people are purely self-motivated.

questions.stem: Select the one-word substitution for: a person who walks about during sleep without any conscious awareness of doing so.

options.option_text: Insomniac — one who cannot fall or stay asleep
Somnambulist — one who walks while still asleep
Narcoleptic — one prone to sudden deep sleep attacks
Hypochondriac — one excessively anxious about their health

questions.explanation: Somnambulist derives from Latin somnus (sleep) and ambulare (to walk), precisely meaning a sleepwalker. Insomniac is the most tempting distractor because it relates to sleep, but it describes someone who cannot sleep — the exact opposite of the condition described in the stem.

questions.stem: Select the one-word substitution for: a word or name formed by rearranging all the letters of another existing word or name.

options.option_text: Palindrome — a word reading the same forward and backward
Acronym — a word formed from the initial letters of a phrase
Anagram — a word formed by rearranging letters of another
Onomatopoeia — a word that phonetically imitates a natural sound

questions.explanation: An anagram involves rearranging every letter of a word to form a new word, e.g., 'listen' rearranged becomes 'silent'. Palindrome is the most common distractor — it reads identically in both directions (e.g., 'madam') but requires no rearrangement and the letter order itself is the defining feature.

questions.stem: Select the one-word substitution for: an intense and irrational fear of open spaces, crowded areas, or public situations from which escape seems difficult.

options.option_text: Claustrophobia — fear of enclosed or tightly confined spaces
Acrophobia — fear of heights or elevated positions
Agoraphobia — fear of open spaces or public situations
Arachnophobia — fear of spiders and related arachnids

questions.explanation: Agoraphobia comes from Greek agora (marketplace/open assembly) and phobos (fear); it describes dread of open or public environments. Claustrophobia is the classic distractor because it is also a space-related phobia — but it is precisely the opposite, referring to enclosed rather than open spaces.

questions.stem: Select the one-word substitution for: the art of producing visually elegant and decorative handwriting or lettering using a special pen or brush.

options.option_text: Typography — the technique of arranging and designing printed type
Stenography — the skill of rapid writing using shorthand symbols
Lithography — a printing process using a flat stone or metal plate
Calligraphy — the art of producing ornate and elegant handwriting

questions.explanation: Calligraphy (Greek kallos = beauty, graphia = writing) specifically means decorative, artistic handwriting executed with a brush or nib. Typography is the most tempting distractor because it also involves letterforms and aesthetics, but it refers to the design and arrangement of mechanically printed type, not hand-drawn writing.

questions.stem: Select the one-word substitution for: a statement that appears self-contradictory or logically absurd on the surface yet, upon reflection, expresses a possible truth.

options.option_text: Oxymoron — a figure joining two directly contradictory words together
Tautology — needless repetition of the same idea in different words
Euphemism — a mild phrase substituted for a harsh or blunt one
Paradox — a seemingly absurd proposition that may contain deep truth

questions.explanation: A paradox is a complete proposition or statement that contradicts itself yet may reveal a deeper truth (e.g., 'The more you know, the more you realise you know nothing'). Oxymoron is the most frequent distractor — it also involves contradiction, but only at the level of two compressed opposing words or phrases (e.g., 'bitter-sweet'), not a full self-contradictory statement.

questions.stem: Select the one-word substitution for: a formal public speech or written composition that lavishes elaborate praise on a particular person, event, or achievement.

options.option_text: Eulogy — a tribute speech typically delivered at a funeral service
Elegy — a reflective poem composed to mourn the death of someone
Panegyric — an elaborate oration or text lavishing the highest praise
Encomium — a formal written or spoken expression of glowing praise

questions.explanation: Panegyric (Greek panēgyrikos, from pan = all + agora = assembly) denotes extravagant public praise not confined to any specific occasion. Eulogy is the chief distractor since it is also a speech of praise — but a eulogy is specifically associated with honouring the recently deceased at a funeral, whereas a panegyric praises the living or an achievement in any public forum.

questions.stem: Select the one-word substitution for: a diplomat who has been formally vested with full and independent authority to represent their government and conclude binding international treaties.

options.option_text: Emissary — an agent dispatched on a specific diplomatic mission
Envoy — a government representative assigned to a foreign country
Ambassador — a nation's highest-ranking permanent diplomatic official
Plenipotentiary — a diplomat vested with full independent treaty power

questions.explanation: Plenipotentiary derives from Latin pleni (full) + potens (power); it names a diplomat who holds unrestricted authority to conclude treaties in the name of their state without needing further approval. Ambassador is the most tempting distractor — an ambassador is the senior permanent representative of a country, but the role does not inherently carry full autonomous treaty-making authority, which is what distinguishes a plenipotentiary.
